slides.title: Antifungal classes and mechanisms
rows: Inhibit fungal lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase (CYP51), reducing ergosterol synthesis.
Spectrum and human CYP interactions differ substantially within the class. Fluconazole lacks Aspergillus and Mucorales activity.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Antifungal classes and mechanisms Mechanisms of action Class Target Bedside implication Triazoles Inhibit fungal lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase (CYP51), reducing ergosterol synthesis. Spectrum and human CYP interactions differ substantially within the class. Fluconazole lacks Aspergillus and Mucorales activity. Echinocandins Inhibit beta-1,3-D-glucan synthase in the cell wall. Active against many Candida species. Aspergillus activity does not make micafungin standard primary monotherapy for invasive aspergillosis. No useful Cryptococcus or Mucorales coverage. Amphotericin B Binds ergosterol and disrupts fungal membranes. Broad yeast and mold activity, with clinically important resistant species. Formulation determines toxicity and distribution. Flucytosine Converted within fungal cells into metabolites that interfere with RNA and DNA synthesis. Good CNS entry; rapid resistance with monotherapy limits its role to selected combination regimens. [4] [2] [11] [19] Coverage of echinocandins, polyenes, and flucytosine Class and example drug Yeast role Mold role Coverage pitfall Echinocandin: micafungin (Mycamine) Initial Candida treatment, including many azole-resistant isolates. Aspergillus salvage or selected combination use. No useful Cryptococcus or Mucorales activity. Trichosporon is another important gap. Polyene: liposomal amphotericin B (AmBisome) Candida and Cryptococcus treatment roles. Aspergillus and Mucorales activity. A. terreus commonly has amphotericin resistance; rare molds need species-specific evaluation. Antimetabolite: flucytosine (Ancobon) Selected Candida and Cryptococcus combinations. Not a broad mold drug. Do not use as routine monotherapy. [1] [2] [19] [11]

slides.title: Coverage of echinocandins, polyenes, and flucytosine
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Antifungal classes and mechanisms Mechanisms of action Class Target Bedside implication Triazoles Inhibit fungal lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase (CYP51), reducing ergosterol synthesis. Spectrum and human CYP interactions differ substantially within the class. Fluconazole lacks Aspergillus and Mucorales activity. Echinocandins Inhibit beta-1,3-D-glucan synthase in the cell wall. Active against many Candida species. Aspergillus activity does not make micafungin standard primary monotherapy for invasive aspergillosis. No useful Cryptococcus or Mucorales coverage. Amphotericin B Binds ergosterol and disrupts fungal membranes. Broad yeast and mold activity, with clinically important resistant species. Formulation determines toxicity and distribution. Flucytosine Converted within fungal cells into metabolites that interfere with RNA and DNA synthesis. Good CNS entry; rapid resistance with monotherapy limits its role to selected combination regimens. [4] [2] [11] [19] Coverage of echinocandins, polyenes, and flucytosine Class and example drug Yeast role Mold role Coverage pitfall Echinocandin: micafungin (Mycamine) Initial Candida treatment, including many azole-resistant isolates. Aspergillus salvage or selected combination use. No useful Cryptococcus or Mucorales activity. Trichosporon is another important gap. Polyene: liposomal amphotericin B (AmBisome) Candida and Cryptococcus treatment roles. Aspergillus and Mucorales activity. A. terreus commonly has amphotericin resistance; rare molds need species-specific evaluation. Antimetabolite: flucytosine (Ancobon) Selected Candida and Cryptococcus combinations. Not a broad mold drug. Do not use as routine monotherapy. [1] [2] [19] [11]

slides.title: Azole spectrum
paragraphs: Azoles are listed by first U.S. approval year. Later agents retain yeast activity while adding coverage of some molds. Species, resistance, and the clinical indication determine which drug is appropriate.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Azole spectrum Azoles are listed by first U.S. approval year. Later agents retain yeast activity while adding coverage of some molds. Species, resistance, and the clinical indication determine which drug is appropriate. Azole coverage across yeasts and opportunistic molds Azole / approval Candida Cryptococcus Aspergillus Dematiaceous molds Mucorales Fluconazole 1990 Active* Standard* No Unreliable No Itraconazole 1992 Active* Alternative* Active* Many species* Unreliable Voriconazole 2002 Active* Salvage* Active* Many species* No Posaconazole 2006 Active* Salvage* Active* Many species* Active* Isavuconazole 2015 In vitro* Salvage* Active* Variable; limited data* Active* Green Established activity or a usual clinical role in the specified setting. Amber Alternative/salvage use, reduced effectiveness, or limited clinical evidence. Red Absent or unreliable coverage. *See the organism-specific notes and susceptibility table. Cryptococcus : fluconazole has established roles in selected pulmonary disease and in consolidation/maintenance after appropriate induction. CNS or disseminated disease usually requires an amphotericin-based induction regimen with flucytosine. Itraconazole is an inferior consolidation alternative; voriconazole, posaconazole, and isavuconazole are selected alternatives or salvage agents with much less evidence. [37] [38] Suspected invasive mold disease while receiving voriconazole prophylaxis requires consideration of Mucorales, resistant Aspergillus, inadequate exposure, and other molds. Increasing the voriconazole dose does not add Mucorales activity. Aspergillus azole resistance may affect several agents; susceptibility testing should guide a change within the class.

paragraphs: Azole selection differs among Histoplasma, Blastomyces, and Coccidioides. The table applies when treatment is indicated. Severe disease may require amphotericin induction.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Azole activity against endemic fungi Azole selection differs among Histoplasma, Blastomyces, and Coccidioides. The table applies when treatment is indicated. Severe disease may require amphotericin induction. Azole roles in selected endemic dimorphic infections Azole Histoplasma Blastomyces Coccidioides Fluconazole Less effective* Less effective* Standard* Itraconazole Preferred azole* Preferred azole* Standard* Voriconazole Not preferred; early mortality concern* [56] Alternative; CNS role* Salvage* Posaconazole Alternative* Limited/salvage* Salvage* Isavuconazole Limited data* Limited data* Alternative/salvage* Do not substitute voriconazole routinely for itraconazole in histoplasmosis Itraconazole remains the preferred azole. Voriconazole has antifungal activity against Histoplasma, but a retrospective comparison found higher early mortality with voriconazole. It should not be used as a routine substitute for itraconazole. [56] [12] [39] [40] [41] [42] Treatment considerations Coccidioides : fluconazole is a standard option, including for meningitis; itraconazole has established roles, particularly in selected nonmeningeal disease. Voriconazole, posaconazole, and isavuconazole have alternative/salvage experience. The fluconazole mold gap in the first table refers to molds such as Aspergillus and Mucorales, not to absence of activity against Coccidioides. [41] [42] Fellow teaching Dematiaceous molds

slides.title: Azole activity against endemic fungi
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Azole activity against endemic fungi Azole selection differs among Histoplasma, Blastomyces, and Coccidioides. The table applies when treatment is indicated. Severe disease may require amphotericin induction. Azole roles in selected endemic dimorphic infections Azole Histoplasma Blastomyces Coccidioides Fluconazole Less effective* Less effective* Standard* Itraconazole Preferred azole* Preferred azole* Standard* Voriconazole Not preferred; early mortality concern* [56] Alternative; CNS role* Salvage* Posaconazole Alternative* Limited/salvage* Salvage* Isavuconazole Limited data* Limited data* Alternative/salvage* Do not substitute voriconazole routinely for itraconazole in histoplasmosis Itraconazole remains the preferred azole. Voriconazole has antifungal activity against Histoplasma, but a retrospective comparison found higher early mortality with voriconazole. It should not be used as a routine substitute for itraconazole. [56] [12] [39] [40] [41] [42] Treatment considerations Coccidioides : fluconazole is a standard option, including for meningitis; itraconazole has established roles, particularly in selected nonmeningeal disease. Voriconazole, posaconazole, and isavuconazole have alternative/salvage experience. The fluconazole mold gap in the first table refers to molds such as Aspergillus and Mucorales, not to absence of activity against Coccidioides. [41] [42] Fellow teaching Dematiaceous molds

slides.title: Candida species and susceptibility
paragraphs: Species are grouped by usual fluconazole susceptibility, followed by C. auris. Individual isolates may differ. Use the reported susceptibility category and infection site to guide treatment; SDD means susceptible-dose dependent.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Candida species and susceptibility Species are grouped by usual fluconazole susceptibility, followed by C. auris. Individual isolates may differ. Use the reported susceptibility category and infection site to guide treatment; SDD means susceptible-dose dependent. Species Azoles, especially fluconazole Echinocandins Amphotericin B Usually fluconazole susceptible; acquired resistance remains possible C. albicans Usually fluconazole susceptible; confirm the isolate. Usually active. Usually active; toxicity often favors other options. C. tropicalis Often susceptible, but azole resistance varies by region and exposure. Usually active; acquired resistance is possible. Usually active. C. parapsilosis Often susceptible historically, but resistant strains and outbreaks are increasingly reported. Higher baseline MICs than many Candida species; this is not automatic clinical resistance. Usually active. C. lusitaniae May be active; acquired resistance can occur. Often active; acquired resistance can occur. Can develop amphotericin resistance during therapy. Repeat susceptibility testing if infection persists. Reduced fluconazole susceptibility: SDD or resistant, depending on the isolate C. glabrata Nakaseomyces glabratus Reduced susceptibility/resistance is common. High-dose fluconazole step-down only when the MIC category supports it. Usual initial invasive-infection choice, but acquired FKS resistance can occur. Potential option for resistant isolates; confirm susceptibility. Intrinsic fluconazole resistance C. krusei Pichia kudriavzevii Intrinsic fluconazole resistance does not mean resistance to every azole. Voriconazole can be selected step-down therapy. Usually active. Clinical alternative; review susceptibility rather than assuming all isolates are susceptible. Frequent fluconazole resistance; possible resistance to multiple classes C. auris Candidozyma auris Fluconazole resistance is common. Resistance can involve multiple drug classes; resistance may extend to newer azoles. Usual initial adult therapy. Echinocandin resistance and pan-resistance occur. Variable susceptibility; selected alternative for echinocandin resistance or clinical nonresponse. [1] [49] [50] [45] [46] Fellow teaching Species and MIC interpretation

slides.title: Candida auris
paragraphs: For adult clinical infection, CDC recommends an echinocandin initially, for example micafungin 100 mg IV daily. Send susceptibility testing and reassess the clinical response. Consider liposomal amphotericin B 5 mg/kg/day for echinocandin resistance or lack of improvement after 5 days, while reassessing source control and the diagnosis. Pan-resistant infection warrants expert/reference-laboratory input and consideration of investigational access. [45]
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Candida auris For adult clinical infection, CDC recommends an echinocandin initially, for example micafungin 100 mg IV daily. Send susceptibility testing and reassess the clinical response. Consider liposomal amphotericin B 5 mg/kg/day for echinocandin resistance or lack of improvement after 5 days, while reassessing source control and the diagnosis. Pan-resistant infection warrants expert/reference-laboratory input and consideration of investigational access. [45] Do not treat asymptomatic colonization or attempt antifungal decolonization. Notify infection prevention and public health promptly. In acute care use Contact Precautions, clean shared equipment, and use an EPA List P disinfectant. Communicate status on transfer. Clearing an infection does not mean colonization has cleared. [48] [47] Fellow teaching C. auris susceptibility thresholds

paragraphs: Do not treat asymptomatic colonization or attempt antifungal decolonization. Notify infection prevention and public health promptly. In acute care use Contact Precautions, clean shared equipment, and use an EPA List P disinfectant. Communicate status on transfer. Clearing an infection does not mean colonization has cleared. Fellow teaching C. auris susceptibility thresholds

Complete source section:
Candida auris For adult clinical infection, CDC recommends an echinocandin initially, for example micafungin 100 mg IV daily. Send susceptibility testing and reassess the clinical response. Consider liposomal amphotericin B 5 mg/kg/day for echinocandin resistance or lack of improvement after 5 days, while reassessing source control and the diagnosis. Pan-resistant infection warrants expert/reference-laboratory input and consideration of investigational access. [45] Do not treat asymptomatic colonization or attempt antifungal decolonization. slides.title: Fluconazole / Diflucan
paragraphs: Oral absorption is reliable; use oral therapy when the patient can absorb it. Renal clearance makes maintenance dose adjustment important. It reaches urine and CSF well.

Nausea and headache are common. Watch liver injury and QT prolongation. Less common effects include severe skin reactions, reversible alopecia with prolonged treatment, and reported adrenal insufficiency. Warfarin and other CYP substrates still require review. [4]
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Azole administration and adverse effects Fluconazole / Diflucan Oral absorption is reliable; use oral therapy when the patient can absorb it. Renal clearance makes maintenance dose adjustment important. It reaches urine and CSF well. Nausea and headache are common. Watch liver injury and QT prolongation. Less common effects include severe skin reactions, reversible alopecia with prolonged treatment, and reported adrenal insufficiency. Warfarin and other CYP substrates still require review. [4] Itraconazole / Sporanox; SUBA formulation / Tolsura Conventional capsules depend on food and gastric acidity. Solution is better absorbed fasting. SUBA formulations have different dosing and administration instructions. They are not interchangeable milligram for milligram. GI intolerance and liver injury can occur. Negative inotropic effects can cause edema or heart failure. Peripheral neuropathy, hearing loss, and pseudohyperaldosteronism are additional reported toxicities. New dyspnea or edema warrants evaluation for heart failure. [5] [3] Voriconazole / Vfend Take oral doses at least an hour before or after food. Variable CYP2C19 metabolism and nonlinear kinetics make TDM central to treatment. Transient visual changes are common. Hallucinations or encephalopathy may reflect excessive exposure. Also watch liver injury and QT prolongation. Prolonged treatment is associated with photosensitivity, cutaneous malignancy, and fluoride-associated periostitis. Bone pain with elevated alkaline phosphatase should prompt consideration of periostitis. Recommend sun protection and skin surveillance during prolonged treatment. [6] Posaconazole / Noxafil Delayed-release tablets or IV generally give more dependable exposure than conventional suspension. Suspension absorption depends on food and gastric conditions; do not substitute the formulations using the same dose. GI effects, liver injury, and QT prolongation occur. Hypertension plus hypokalemia can represent pseudohyperaldosteronism, often with low renin and aldosterone. Check BP, potassium, and posaconazole levels; reassess the antifungal if pseudohyperaldosteronism is suspected. [7] [35] Isavuconazonium / Cresemba Isavuconazonium is converted to active isavuconazole. 372 mg isavuconazonium sulfate equals 200 mg isavuconazole. Oral absorption is reliable and not materially food dependent; IV does not require cyclodextrin. It shortens QT and is contraindicated in familial short-QT syndrome. GI symptoms and liver abnormalities occur; serious hypersensitivity is possible. It often has fewer visual/skin effects than voriconazole, but retains clinically important CYP3A interactions. [8] [20] Oral voriconazole does not require renal dose reduction. IV voriconazole and IV posaconazole contain SBECD, which can accumulate in renal impairment. Product labels favor avoiding these IV formulations below the specified renal threshold unless benefit outweighs risk. Consider oral therapy and monitor renal function. [6] [7]

New dyspnea or edema warrants evaluation for heart failure. [5] [3] Voriconazole / Vfend Take oral doses at least an hour before or after food. Variable CYP2C19 metabolism and nonlinear kinetics make TDM central to treatment. Transient visual changes are common. Hallucinations or encephalopathy may reflect excessive exposure. Also watch liver injury and QT prolongation. Prolonged treatment is associated with photosensitivity, cutaneous malignancy, and fluoride-associated periostitis. Bone pain with elevated alkaline phosphatase should prompt consideration of periostitis. Recommend sun protection and skin surveillance during prolonged treatment. [6] Posaconazole / Noxafil Delayed-release tablets or IV generally give more dependable exposure than conventional suspension. Suspension absorption depends on food and gastric conditions; do not substitute the formulations using the same dose. GI effects, liver injury, and QT prolongation occur. Hypertension plus hypokalemia can represent pseudohyperaldosteronism, often with low renin and aldosterone. Check BP, potassium, and posaconazole levels; reassess the antifungal if pseudohyperaldosteronism is suspected. [7] [35] Isavuconazonium / Cresemba Isavuconazonium is converted to active isavuconazole. 372 mg isavuconazonium sulfate equals 200 mg isavuconazole. Oral absorption is reliable and not materially food dependent; IV does not require cyclodextrin. It shortens QT and is contraindicated in familial short-QT syndrome. GI symptoms and liver abnormalities occur; serious hypersensitivity is possible. It often has fewer visual/skin effects than voriconazole, but retains clinically important CYP3A interactions. [8] [20] Oral voriconazole does not require renal dose reduction. IV voriconazole and IV posaconazole contain SBECD, which can accumulate in renal impairment. Product labels favor avoiding these IV formulations below the specified renal threshold unless benefit outweighs risk. Consider oral therapy and monitor renal function. [6] [7]

slides.title: Echinocandins, including micafungin
paragraphs: Micafungin is IV only. It usually needs neither renal nor hepatic dose adjustment under U.S. labeling, and no dialysis replacement dose. It has fewer CYP interactions than azoles; review concomitant medications. Routine drug levels are not standard. [9]

For candidemia, an echinocandin is a usual initial choice. Fluconazole step-down requires a clinically stable patient, susceptible isolate, and cleared blood cultures. Infected devices and undrained foci still need source control. [1]

slides.title: Amphotericin B formulations and adverse effects
slides.section: Amphotericin B formulations and adverse effects
paragraphs: Write the full formulation in the order. Liposomal amphotericin B, amphotericin B lipid complex, and deoxycholate differ in dose and toxicity. They are not interchangeable. Liposomal amphotericin reduces, but does not remove, nephrotoxicity and infusion reactions. [10]

Follow creatinine, potassium, magnesium, CBC, and liver tests. Check renal function and electrolytes daily initially, replace potassium and magnesium as needed, and review other nephrotoxic drugs. Consider saline hydration if volume status allows. Prepare and dilute the drug according to the formulation's label; saline hydration and the drug infusion are separate orders.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Amphotericin B formulations and adverse effects Write the full formulation in the order. Liposomal amphotericin B, amphotericin B lipid complex, and deoxycholate differ in dose and toxicity. They are not interchangeable. Liposomal amphotericin reduces, but does not remove, nephrotoxicity and infusion reactions. [10] Follow creatinine, potassium, magnesium, CBC, and liver tests. Check renal function and electrolytes daily initially, replace potassium and magnesium as needed, and review other nephrotoxic drugs. Consider saline hydration if volume status allows. Prepare and dilute the drug according to the formulation's label; saline hydration and the drug infusion are separate orders. Common problems include AKI, potassium/magnesium wasting, infusion fever or rigors, and anemia. Less common serious events include hypersensitivity, chest/back pain during infusion, and arrhythmias, including those promoted by electrolyte disturbances. Unexpected phosphate elevation with AmBisome may be assay interference. [10] Amphotericin formulation matters for urinary infection. See the urinary exposure table ; liposomal amphotericin is not a substitute for deoxycholate in this setting. Flucytosine / Ancobon Flucytosine reaches the CNS and is used in selected combination induction regimens. Renal accumulation can cause marrow suppression and hepatotoxicity; GI intolerance is also common. Adjust for renal function and dialysis. Follow CBC, renal function, and liver tests closely, especially when amphotericin worsens renal clearance. [11]

slides.title: Amphotericin B formulations and adverse effects
slides.section: Amphotericin B formulations and adverse effects
paragraphs: Common problems include AKI, potassium/magnesium wasting, infusion fever or rigors, and anemia. Less common serious events include hypersensitivity, chest/back pain during infusion, and arrhythmias, including those promoted by electrolyte disturbances. Unexpected phosphate elevation with AmBisome may be assay interference. [10]
Amphotericin formulation matters for urinary infection. See the urinary exposure table ; liposomal amphotericin is not a substitute for deoxycholate in this setting.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Amphotericin B formulations and adverse effects Write the full formulation in the order. Liposomal amphotericin B, amphotericin B lipid complex, and deoxycholate differ in dose and toxicity. They are not interchangeable. Liposomal amphotericin reduces, but does not remove, nephrotoxicity and infusion reactions. [10] Follow creatinine, potassium, magnesium, CBC, and liver tests. Check renal function and electrolytes daily initially, replace potassium and magnesium as needed, and review other nephrotoxic drugs. Consider saline hydration if volume status allows. Prepare and dilute the drug according to the formulation's label; saline hydration and the drug infusion are separate orders. Common problems include AKI, potassium/magnesium wasting, infusion fever or rigors, and anemia. Less common serious events include hypersensitivity, chest/back pain during infusion, and arrhythmias, including those promoted by electrolyte disturbances. Unexpected phosphate elevation with AmBisome may be assay interference. [10] Amphotericin formulation matters for urinary infection. See the urinary exposure table ; liposomal amphotericin is not a substitute for deoxycholate in this setting. Flucytosine / Ancobon Flucytosine reaches the CNS and is used in selected combination induction regimens. Renal accumulation can cause marrow suppression and hepatotoxicity; GI intolerance is also common. Adjust for renal function and dialysis. Follow CBC, renal function, and liver tests closely, especially when amphotericin worsens renal clearance. [11]

slides.title: CNS penetration
paragraphs: CNS selection depends on the organism, clinical evidence, and drug exposure. CSF concentrations and brain tissue concentrations may differ.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
CNS penetration CNS selection depends on the organism, clinical evidence, and drug exposure. CSF concentrations and brain tissue concentrations may differ. Drug Size / binding CNS finding Practical interpretation Fluconazole Small, about 306 Da; relatively water soluble; about 11-12% bound. CSF approximately 80% of plasma in fungal meningitis. No Aspergillus activity despite good CSF exposure. Voriconazole Small, about 349 Da; about 58% bound. Human CSF/plasma median 0.46 in a small PK study; brain entry demonstrated. Established preferred azole for CNS aspergillosis when the organism is susceptible. Itraconazole Large, about 706 Da; lipophilic; 99.8% bound. Low CSF concentrations despite substantial tissue distribution. Do not substitute for voriconazole in CNS aspergillosis on spectrum alone. Posaconazole Large, about 701 Da; lipophilic; >98% bound. CSF exposure often low and variable. Selected CNS salvage use needs organism, exposure, and clinical evidence; serum levels do not directly measure brain exposure. Isavuconazole Active drug is smaller than itraconazole/posaconazole; >99% bound. Brain tissue exposure has been demonstrated despite limited CSF exposure. Potential CNS use is organism-specific; human evidence is much smaller than for voriconazole in CNS aspergillosis. [4] [6] [5] [7] [8] [15] [16] [17] [18] Fellow teaching See molecular structures and the pharmacology behind these differences. Fellow teaching CSF versus brain tissue

slides.title: Candiduria and urinary drug concentrations
paragraphs: Candiduria alone does not establish infection. Asymptomatic candiduria usually needs risk-factor and catheter management, not an antifungal. IDSA exceptions include neutropenia, very low-birth-weight infants, and planned urologic manipulation. Diabetes or a chronic catheter alone is not an indication to treat.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Candiduria and urinary drug concentrations Candiduria alone does not establish infection. Asymptomatic candiduria usually needs risk-factor and catheter management, not an antifungal. IDSA exceptions include neutropenia, very low-birth-weight infants, and planned urologic manipulation. Diabetes or a chronic catheter alone is not an indication to treat. Presentation Treatment decision Asymptomatic candiduria Usually observe and remove or replace an unnecessary catheter. Assess the exceptions above. Compatible cystitis symptoms Exclude other causes. If the Candida isolate is fluconazole susceptible, fluconazole is the usual preferred drug. Ascending pyelonephritis or obstructed collecting system Use a urine-active drug guided by susceptibility. Relieve obstruction; consider stent/nephrostomy removal or exchange. Fungus balls generally require intervention. Candidemia with hematogenous renal involvement Treat invasive candidiasis. Micafungin can remain appropriate because renal tissue exposure differs from drug concentration in urine. In catheterized patients, pyuria and colony count cannot reliably distinguish colonization from infection. Unexplained systemic illness, obstruction, or persistent compatible symptoms may warrant further evaluation and imaging. [1] Antifungal concentrations in urine Drug Urinary exposure Practical consequence Fluconazole High active-drug concentrations. Preferred for susceptible Candida urinary infection; adjust maintenance dosing for renal function. Micafungin and other echinocandins Very poor active-drug excretion into urine. Not routine therapy for Candida cystitis or ascending collecting-system infection. Hematogenous renal infection is a different setting. Voriconazole, itraconazole, posaconazole, isavuconazole Low active-drug urinary exposure. Do not select a mold-active azole for Candida cystitis simply because the isolate appears susceptible. Amphotericin B deoxycholate Useful urinary concentrations. Selected resistant Candida urinary infections; substantial toxicity limits use. Liposomal amphotericin B and other lipid formulations Inadequate urinary concentrations for routine Candida UTI treatment. Not interchangeable with deoxycholate for this indication. Flucytosine High active-drug urinary concentrations. Selected resistant C. glabrata infections; not reliable for C. krusei. Renal accumulation, marrow toxicity, and resistance limit use. [1]

slides.title: Candiduria and urinary drug concentrations
paragraphs: In catheterized patients, pyuria and colony count cannot reliably distinguish colonization from infection. Unexplained systemic illness, obstruction, or persistent compatible symptoms may warrant further evaluation and imaging. [1]
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Candiduria and urinary drug concentrations Candiduria alone does not establish infection. Asymptomatic candiduria usually needs risk-factor and catheter management, not an antifungal. IDSA exceptions include neutropenia, very low-birth-weight infants, and planned urologic manipulation. Diabetes or a chronic catheter alone is not an indication to treat. Presentation Treatment decision Asymptomatic candiduria Usually observe and remove or replace an unnecessary catheter. Assess the exceptions above. Compatible cystitis symptoms Exclude other causes. If the Candida isolate is fluconazole susceptible, fluconazole is the usual preferred drug. Ascending pyelonephritis or obstructed collecting system Use a urine-active drug guided by susceptibility. Relieve obstruction; consider stent/nephrostomy removal or exchange. Fungus balls generally require intervention. Candidemia with hematogenous renal involvement Treat invasive candidiasis. Micafungin can remain appropriate because renal tissue exposure differs from drug concentration in urine. In catheterized patients, pyuria and colony count cannot reliably distinguish colonization from infection. Unexplained systemic illness, obstruction, or persistent compatible symptoms may warrant further evaluation and imaging. [1] Antifungal concentrations in urine Drug Urinary exposure Practical consequence Fluconazole High active-drug concentrations. Preferred for susceptible Candida urinary infection; adjust maintenance dosing for renal function. Micafungin and other echinocandins Very poor active-drug excretion into urine. Not routine therapy for Candida cystitis or ascending collecting-system infection. Hematogenous renal infection is a different setting. Voriconazole, itraconazole, posaconazole, isavuconazole Low active-drug urinary exposure. Do not select a mold-active azole for Candida cystitis simply because the isolate appears susceptible. Amphotericin B deoxycholate Useful urinary concentrations. Selected resistant Candida urinary infections; substantial toxicity limits use. Liposomal amphotericin B and other lipid formulations Inadequate urinary concentrations for routine Candida UTI treatment. Not interchangeable with deoxycholate for this indication. Flucytosine High active-drug urinary concentrations. Selected resistant C. glabrata infections; not reliable for C. krusei. Renal accumulation, marrow toxicity, and resistance limit use. [1]

slides.title: Antifungal concentrations in urine
rows: Do not select a mold-active azole for Candida cystitis simply because the isolate appears susceptible.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Candiduria and urinary drug concentrations Candiduria alone does not establish infection. Asymptomatic candiduria usually needs risk-factor and catheter management, not an antifungal. IDSA exceptions include neutropenia, very low-birth-weight infants, and planned urologic manipulation. Diabetes or a chronic catheter alone is not an indication to treat. Presentation Treatment decision Asymptomatic candiduria Usually observe and remove or replace an unnecessary catheter. Assess the exceptions above. Compatible cystitis symptoms Exclude other causes. If the Candida isolate is fluconazole susceptible, fluconazole is the usual preferred drug. Ascending pyelonephritis or obstructed collecting system Use a urine-active drug guided by susceptibility. Relieve obstruction; consider stent/nephrostomy removal or exchange. Fungus balls generally require intervention. Candidemia with hematogenous renal involvement Treat invasive candidiasis. Micafungin can remain appropriate because renal tissue exposure differs from drug concentration in urine. In catheterized patients, pyuria and colony count cannot reliably distinguish colonization from infection. Unexplained systemic illness, obstruction, or persistent compatible symptoms may warrant further evaluation and imaging. [1] Antifungal concentrations in urine Drug Urinary exposure Practical consequence Fluconazole High active-drug concentrations. Preferred for susceptible Candida urinary infection; adjust maintenance dosing for renal function. Micafungin and other echinocandins Very poor active-drug excretion into urine. Not routine therapy for Candida cystitis or ascending collecting-system infection. Hematogenous renal infection is a different setting. Voriconazole, itraconazole, posaconazole, isavuconazole Low active-drug urinary exposure. Do not select a mold-active azole for Candida cystitis simply because the isolate appears susceptible. Amphotericin B deoxycholate Useful urinary concentrations. Selected resistant Candida urinary infections; substantial toxicity limits use. Liposomal amphotericin B and other lipid formulations Inadequate urinary concentrations for routine Candida UTI treatment. Not interchangeable with deoxycholate for this indication. slides.title: Selected adult doses
paragraphs: The doses below assume normal organ function. Confirm the indication, weight, formulation, hepatic function, and renal replacement requirements before prescribing.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Selected adult doses The doses below assume normal organ function. Confirm the indication, weight, formulation, hepatic function, and renal replacement requirements before prescribing. Drug / example indication Loading and maintenance Common error Fluconazole / selected invasive Candida infection 800 mg (12 mg/kg) once, then 400 mg (6 mg/kg) daily. Higher doses apply to some susceptible isolates or other indications. Omitting a load or forgetting renal maintenance adjustment. Micafungin / candidemia 100 mg IV daily; no routine loading dose. Using 100 mg as a universal dose. Esophageal candidiasis uses 150 mg daily; endocarditis is a separate high-dose strategy. Caspofungin / candidemia 70 mg IV once, then 50 mg daily. Forgetting the loading dose. Hepatic dosing and interactions need individual review. Anidulafungin / candidemia 200 mg IV once, then 100 mg daily. Forgetting the loading dose. Voriconazole / invasive aspergillosis IV 6 mg/kg every 12 h for 2 doses, then 4 mg/kg every 12 h. Oral regimens differ; confirm weight and label, then guide with TDM. Treating the oral and IV regimens as identical mg/kg doses. Posaconazole / adult DR tablet or IV mold regimen 300 mg every 12 h on day 1, then 300 mg daily. Applying this regimen to conventional suspension. Isavuconazonium / adult mold regimen 372 mg every 8 h for 6 doses, then 372 mg daily, starting 12-24 h after the last loading dose. Confusing prodrug milligrams with the 200 mg active-drug equivalent. Liposomal amphotericin B Often 3-5 mg/kg/day for selected invasive infections. Mucormycosis generally 5-10 mg/kg/day; CNS mucormycosis commonly 10 mg/kg/day. Assuming every fungus and compartment needs the same dose. Flucytosine / selected combination induction 25 mg/kg orally every 6 h with normal renal function. Failing to adjust the dose interval as renal function changes. [1] [2] [7] [8] [19] [11]

rows: 100 mg IV daily; no routine loading dose.
Using 100 mg as a universal dose. Esophageal candidiasis uses 150 mg daily; endocarditis is a separate high-dose strategy.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Selected adult doses The doses below assume normal organ function. Confirm the indication, weight, formulation, hepatic function, and renal replacement requirements before prescribing. Drug / example indication Loading and maintenance Common error Fluconazole / selected invasive Candida infection 800 mg (12 mg/kg) once, then 400 mg (6 mg/kg) daily. Higher doses apply to some susceptible isolates or other indications. Omitting a load or forgetting renal maintenance adjustment. Micafungin / candidemia 100 mg IV daily; no routine loading dose. Using 100 mg as a universal dose. Esophageal candidiasis uses 150 mg daily; endocarditis is a separate high-dose strategy. Caspofungin / candidemia 70 mg IV once, then 50 mg daily. Forgetting the loading dose. Hepatic dosing and interactions need individual review. Anidulafungin / candidemia 200 mg IV once, then 100 mg daily. Forgetting the loading dose. Voriconazole / invasive aspergillosis IV 6 mg/kg every 12 h for 2 doses, then 4 mg/kg every 12 h. Oral regimens differ; confirm weight and label, then guide with TDM. Treating the oral and IV regimens as identical mg/kg doses. Posaconazole / adult DR tablet or IV mold regimen 300 mg every 12 h on day 1, then 300 mg daily. Applying this regimen to conventional suspension. Isavuconazonium / adult mold regimen 372 mg every 8 h for 6 doses, then 372 mg daily, starting 12-24 h after the last loading dose. slides.title: Toxicity monitoring and interactions
paragraphs: Obtain baseline renal function, electrolytes, and liver tests for systemic therapy; add CBC when using amphotericin or flucytosine. Review ECG/QTc when an azole or interacting drugs create arrhythmia risk. Correct potassium and magnesium abnormalities. During prolonged azole treatment, repeat liver tests early, often weekly initially, then space them according to stability and the agent's label. Voriconazole labeling specifies at least weekly liver tests for the first month, then monthly if stable. Check BP and potassium on posaconazole or itraconazole.
For amphotericin and flucytosine, renal changes require prompt reassessment of dosing, toxicity, and monitoring frequency. [6] [7] [10] [11]
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Toxicity monitoring and interactions Obtain baseline renal function, electrolytes, and liver tests for systemic therapy; add CBC when using amphotericin or flucytosine. Review ECG/QTc when an azole or interacting drugs create arrhythmia risk. Correct potassium and magnesium abnormalities. During prolonged azole treatment, repeat liver tests early, often weekly initially, then space them according to stability and the agent's label. Voriconazole labeling specifies at least weekly liver tests for the first month, then monthly if stable. Check BP and potassium on posaconazole or itraconazole. For amphotericin and flucytosine, renal changes require prompt reassessment of dosing, toxicity, and monitoring frequency. [6] [7] [10] [11] Check interactions when starting and stopping Review calcineurin/mTOR inhibitors, venetoclax and other targeted cancer therapies, vinca alkaloids, DOACs, warfarin, statins, sedatives, and QT-active drugs. Rifamycins and other strong inducers can cause antifungal underexposure. The interaction can reverse after stopping the azole, requiring another dose adjustment and repeat monitoring. [3]

slides.title: Check interactions when starting and stopping
paragraphs: Review calcineurin/mTOR inhibitors, venetoclax and other targeted cancer therapies, vinca alkaloids, DOACs, warfarin, statins, sedatives, and QT-active drugs. Rifamycins and other strong inducers can cause antifungal underexposure. The interaction can reverse after stopping the azole, requiring another dose adjustment and repeat monitoring. [3]
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Toxicity monitoring and interactions Obtain baseline renal function, electrolytes, and liver tests for systemic therapy; add CBC when using amphotericin or flucytosine. Review ECG/QTc when an azole or interacting drugs create arrhythmia risk. Correct potassium and magnesium abnormalities. During prolonged azole treatment, repeat liver tests early, often weekly initially, then space them according to stability and the agent's label. Voriconazole labeling specifies at least weekly liver tests for the first month, then monthly if stable. Check BP and potassium on posaconazole or itraconazole. For amphotericin and flucytosine, renal changes require prompt reassessment of dosing, toxicity, and monitoring frequency. [6] [7] [10] [11] Check interactions when starting and stopping Review calcineurin/mTOR inhibitors, venetoclax and other targeted cancer therapies, vinca alkaloids, DOACs, warfarin, statins, sedatives, and QT-active drugs. slides.title: Therapeutic drug monitoring
paragraphs: Document the last dose, draw time, formulation, recent missed doses, food/tube feed administration, interacting drugs, and the indication-specific target. mg/L and mcg/mL are numerically equivalent. Repeat a level after a meaningful dose, route, formulation, interaction, absorption, or clinical change. [14]
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Therapeutic drug monitoring Document the last dose, draw time, formulation, recent missed doses, food/tube feed administration, interacting drugs, and the indication-specific target. mg/L and mcg/mL are numerically equivalent. Repeat a level after a meaningful dose, route, formulation, interaction, absorption, or clinical change. [14] Drug Usual first assessment Interpretation Voriconazole A trough at about day 3-5 after loading is common; earlier day 2-3 assessment is possible. Measure the parent drug. Common treatment targets are >1-2 mg/L with an upper boundary around 5-5.5 mg/L; severe/CNS disease often prompts a higher minimum within the range. Targets vary by protocol. Itraconazole About day 5-7 after loading; about day 10-14 without loading. Histoplasmosis, parent-only chromatographic assay: >1 mg/L and generally <3-4 mg/L. Combined itraconazole + hydroxyitraconazole: use the indication-specific protocol. The 2026 IDSA aspergillosis pharmacology appendix lists expert treatment targets >1-2 mg/L and an upper boundary <5 mg/L . These combined thresholds are not interchangeable with the parent-only range. [3] [12] Posaconazole A trough at about day 5-7 after loading. A commonly used prophylaxis target is at least 0.7 mg/L. Treatment targets are commonly >1-1.25 mg/L. An upper safety boundary is less settled; high exposure should prompt toxicity review. Isavuconazole Selective TDM, particularly unexpected failure/toxicity, absorption concerns, or unusual PK. No universally validated therapeutic window. Some centers use routine levels; others do not. Do not import voriconazole targets. Flucytosine When monitoring is indicated, usually a 2-hour post-dose level after about 3 days, sooner with concern for accumulation. This is a peak, not an azole trough. BSMM guidance uses about 50-100 mg/L; avoid sustained levels >100 mg/L because toxicity risk increases. Fluconazole, echinocandins, amphotericin B No routine TDM for standard use. Clinical response and organ/toxicity monitoring remain essential. [3] [14] [13] [22] Itraconazole and hydroxyitraconazole levels Example: itraconazole 0.7 mg/L + hydroxyitraconazole 1.3 mg/L = combined 2.0 mg/L. The result meets a combined target of 2.0 mg/L or greater, but does not meet a parent-only target greater than 1.0 mg/L. Compare the result with the range for that assay. Voriconazole N-oxide has minimal antifungal activity and is not added to the voriconazole trough to determine treatment exposure. [6] [13] Fellow teaching Itraconazole assay targets

rows: About day 5-7 after loading; about day 10-14 without loading.

Common treatment targets are >1-2 mg/L with an upper boundary around 5-5.5 mg/L; severe/CNS disease often prompts a higher minimum within the range. Targets vary by protocol. Treatment targets are commonly >1-1.25 mg/L. An upper safety boundary is less settled; high exposure should prompt toxicity review. Isavuconazole Selective TDM, particularly unexpected failure/toxicity, absorption concerns, or unusual PK. No universally validated therapeutic window. Some centers use routine levels; others do not. Do not import voriconazole targets. Flucytosine When monitoring is indicated, usually a 2-hour post-dose level after about 3 days, sooner with concern for accumulation. This is a peak, not an azole trough. BSMM guidance uses about 50-100 mg/L; avoid sustained levels >100 mg/L because toxicity risk increases. Fluconazole, echinocandins, amphotericin B No routine TDM for standard use. Clinical response and organ/toxicity monitoring remain essential. [3] [14] [13] [22] Itraconazole and hydroxyitraconazole levels Example: itraconazole 0.7 mg/L + hydroxyitraconazole 1.3 mg/L = combined 2.0 mg/L. The result meets a combined target of 2.0 mg/L or greater, but does not meet a parent-only target greater than 1.0 mg/L. Compare the result with the range for that assay. Voriconazole N-oxide has minimal antifungal activity and is not added to the voriconazole trough to determine treatment exposure. [6] [13] Fellow teaching Itraconazole assay targets

slides.title: Case 1. Candida in blood and urine
paragraphs: A critically ill patient has candidemia and candiduria. Is micafungin inadequate because it has low urine levels?

Not necessarily. It is a reasonable initial candidemia drug. Determine whether candiduria is colonization, collecting-system disease, obstruction, or hematogenous renal involvement. A separate symptomatic urinary focus may require a different drug and source control. A positive urine culture alone does not establish a Candida UTI. [1]
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Clinical cases Case 1. Candida in blood and urine A critically ill patient has candidemia and candiduria. Is micafungin inadequate because it has low urine levels? Not necessarily. It is a reasonable initial candidemia drug. Determine whether candiduria is colonization, collecting-system disease, obstruction, or hematogenous renal involvement. A separate symptomatic urinary focus may require a different drug and source control. A positive urine culture alone does not establish a Candida UTI. [1] Case 2. Hallucinations during voriconazole treatment A patient develops hallucinations on day 6 after the voriconazole dose was increased. What should be checked? Check dose history, timing, interacting drugs, liver function, electrolytes, and a correctly timed voriconazole level. Also assess other causes of encephalopathy. Serious toxicity may require holding or changing therapy while results are pending. Nonlinear kinetics mean that doubling the dose can produce more than double the exposure. [6] Case 3. A therapeutic level with new edema A patient receiving itraconazole has a satisfactory combined level but develops edema and dyspnea. Does the drug level exclude toxicity? No. Evaluate for heart failure and reconsider itraconazole promptly. Heart failure can occur despite a therapeutic level. Review interacting calcium channel blockers and other contributors. [5]

slides.title: Azole structures and pharmacokinetics
paragraphs: The triazole ring is the shared pharmacophore. Substituents around that ring change binding to fungal CYP51, lipophilicity, molecular size, protein binding, metabolism, and interactions. These changes can expand antifungal activity without improving CNS exposure.

Small size and a substantial unbound fraction favor access to fluid compartments. Lipophilicity can favor membrane passage and tissue partitioning, but very high lipophilicity can accompany extensive protein binding and low CSF concentrations. Efflux, ionization, inflammation, and the measured compartment also matter. Structure alone does not reliably predict CNS exposure.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Azole structures and pharmacokinetics The triazole ring is the shared pharmacophore. Substituents around that ring change binding to fungal CYP51, lipophilicity, molecular size, protein binding, metabolism, and interactions. These changes can expand antifungal activity without improving CNS exposure. Small size and a substantial unbound fraction favor access to fluid compartments. Lipophilicity can favor membrane passage and tissue partitioning, but very high lipophilicity can accompany extensive protein binding and low CSF concentrations. Efflux, ionization, inflammation, and the measured compartment also matter. Structure alone does not reliably predict CNS exposure. Triazole rings and side chains Blue highlights the triazole ring(s); amber highlights other aromatic ring systems. Unhighlighted atoms and linkers also contribute to the side chains. The colors mark structural regions, not polarity. The drawings are not to scale. Fluconazole 306.27 Da END OF HEADER Two triazole rings and a compact substituent framework. Low protein binding and relatively water-soluble disposition favor fluid-compartment exposure. [51] Voriconazole 349.31 Da END OF HEADER One triazole ring; a fluorinated pyrimidine replaces one of fluconazole's triazole-containing arms. It remains relatively small and has established CSF and brain penetration. [52] Itraconazole 705.6 Da END OF HEADER Multiple rings joined by a long substituent chain. Its large size, lipophilicity, and very high binding accompany low CSF exposure. The marketed drug is a stereoisomer mixture; this PubChem representation does not show every component. [53] Posaconazole 700.8 Da END OF HEADER A long ring-and-linker structure related to itraconazole. Substituent changes affect spectrum and disposition; greater mold activity does not imply better CSF penetration. [54] Isavuconazole 437.5 Da END OF HEADER One triazole plus a thiazole-containing substituent. The drawing is active isavuconazole, not the larger isavuconazonium prodrug. High binding coexists with documented infected-brain tissue exposure. [55]

slides.title: Fluconazole 306.27 Da
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Azole structures and pharmacokinetics The triazole ring is the shared pharmacophore. Substituents around that ring change binding to fungal CYP51, lipophilicity, molecular size, protein binding, metabolism, and interactions. These changes can expand antifungal activity without improving CNS exposure. Small size and a substantial unbound fraction favor access to fluid compartments. Lipophilicity can favor membrane passage and tissue partitioning, but very high lipophilicity can accompany extensive protein binding and low CSF concentrations. Efflux, ionization, inflammation, and the measured compartment also matter. Structure alone does not reliably predict CNS exposure. Triazole rings and side chains Blue highlights the triazole ring(s); amber highlights other aromatic ring systems. Unhighlighted atoms and linkers also contribute to the side chains. The colors mark structural regions, not polarity. The drawings are not to scale. Fluconazole 306.27 Da END OF HEADER Two triazole rings and a compact substituent framework. Low protein binding and relatively water-soluble disposition favor fluid-compartment exposure. [51] Voriconazole 349.31 Da END OF HEADER One triazole ring; a fluorinated pyrimidine replaces one of fluconazole's triazole-containing arms. It remains relatively small and has established CSF and brain penetration. [52] Itraconazole 705.6 Da END OF HEADER Multiple rings joined by a long substituent chain. Its large size, lipophilicity, and very high binding accompany low CSF exposure. The marketed drug is a stereoisomer mixture; this PubChem representation does not show every component. [53] Posaconazole 700.8 Da END OF HEADER A long ring-and-linker structure related to itraconazole. Substituent changes affect spectrum and disposition; greater mold activity does not imply better CSF penetration. [54] Isavuconazole 437.5 Da END OF HEADER One triazole plus a thiazole-containing substituent. The drawing is active isavuconazole, not the larger isavuconazonium prodrug. High binding coexists with documented infected-brain tissue exposure. [55]

slides.title: Voriconazole 349.31 Da
paragraphs: One triazole ring; a fluorinated pyrimidine replaces one of fluconazole's triazole-containing arms. It remains relatively small and has established CSF and brain penetration. [52]
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Azole structures and pharmacokinetics The triazole ring is the shared pharmacophore. Substituents around that ring change binding to fungal CYP51, lipophilicity, molecular size, protein binding, metabolism, and interactions. These changes can expand antifungal activity without improving CNS exposure. Small size and a substantial unbound fraction favor access to fluid compartments. Lipophilicity can favor membrane passage and tissue partitioning, but very high lipophilicity can accompany extensive protein binding and low CSF concentrations. Efflux, ionization, inflammation, and the measured compartment also matter. Structure alone does not reliably predict CNS exposure. Triazole rings and side chains Blue highlights the triazole ring(s); amber highlights other aromatic ring systems. Unhighlighted atoms and linkers also contribute to the side chains. The colors mark structural regions, not polarity. The drawings are not to scale. Fluconazole 306.27 Da END OF HEADER Two triazole rings and a compact substituent framework. Low protein binding and relatively water-soluble disposition favor fluid-compartment exposure. [51] Voriconazole 349.31 Da END OF HEADER One triazole ring; a fluorinated pyrimidine replaces one of fluconazole's triazole-containing arms. It remains relatively small and has established CSF and brain penetration. [52] Itraconazole 705.6 Da END OF HEADER Multiple rings joined by a long substituent chain. Its large size, lipophilicity, and very high binding accompany low CSF exposure. The marketed drug is a stereoisomer mixture; this PubChem representation does not show every component. [53] Posaconazole 700.8 Da END OF HEADER A long ring-and-linker structure related to itraconazole. Substituent changes affect spectrum and disposition; greater mold activity does not imply better CSF penetration. [54] Isavuconazole 437.5 Da END OF HEADER One triazole plus a thiazole-containing substituent. The drawing is active isavuconazole, not the larger isavuconazonium prodrug. High binding coexists with documented infected-brain tissue exposure. [55]

slides.title: Advanced clinical considerations
paragraphs: Fellow teaching
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Advanced clinical considerations Fellow teaching Species-specific susceptibility interpretation For C. glabrata, CLSI fluconazole results use susceptible-dose dependent or resistant categories rather than a standard susceptible category. A susceptible-dose dependent result requires an appropriate dose and exposure. Prior echinocandin treatment or persistent infection should prompt echinocandin testing and repeat evaluation for resistance. For C. parapsilosis, use species-specific interpretation: a naturally higher MIC does not by itself mean an echinocandin will fail. [1] Fellow teaching C. auris susceptibility thresholds CDC's tentative resistance thresholds include fluconazole MIC at least 32 mg/L, amphotericin B at least 2 mg/L, and micafungin at least 4 mg/L. They are interim guides with uncertain outcome correlation, not universal susceptible breakpoints. The October 2026 CDC page notes an established CLSI C. auris-specific rezafungin breakpoint, in addition to the tentative thresholds for other agents. Ask the laboratory which method and interpretive standard it uses; do not transfer thresholds between drugs or methods. [46] Fellow teaching Dematiaceous molds Melanized molds such as Alternaria, Curvularia, Exophiala, and Cladophialophora differ in susceptibility, syndrome, and optimal therapy. Itraconazole, voriconazole, and posaconazole have activity against many species, with species-specific variation. Isavuconazole has variable in vitro activity with less clinical evidence; fluconazole is unreliable. CNS disease requires attention to penetration, species identification, susceptibility results, and surgical source control. Isavuconazole susceptibility cannot be inferred from results for voriconazole or posaconazole. [43] [44] The VITAL cryptococcosis/endemic-fungus subset included only 38 patients across five genera and had no randomized comparator. Comparative efficacy for each organism remains uncertain. [42] Fellow teaching Echinocandin resistance FKS mutations can confer class resistance. Prior echinocandin exposure, persistent candidemia, and species identification affect the need for susceptibility testing. C. parapsilosis has higher baseline echinocandin MICs, but that alone does not establish treatment failure. Request susceptibility data and interpret the breakpoint for that species and drug. [1] Fellow teaching CSF and brain tissue concentrations Meningitis, an angioinvasive lesion, and an encapsulated abscess are different compartments. Isavuconazole tissue measurements from two patients showed substantially different concentrations in inflamed versus normal brain. Amphotericin B can be effective in CNS infection despite low CSF levels. A concentration in homogenized tissue does not establish free extracellular exposure or comparative clinical efficacy. [16] [1] Fellow teaching Parent-only and combined itraconazole targets The 2026 IDSA aspergillosis pharmacology appendix describes combined parent-plus-hydroxy targets, whereas current IDSA histoplasmosis guidance favors a parent component >1 mg/L and <3-4 mg/L, and states that a universal combined cutoff has not been established. It notes that combined levels >2 mg/L may provide similar responses to parent levels >1 mg/L. Mayo also provides distinct parent and combined interpretation. State the assay and treatment target explicitly. A combined result can meet its target while the parent level remains below a parent-only target. [3] [12] [13]

slides.title: C. auris susceptibility thresholds
paragraphs: CDC's tentative resistance thresholds include fluconazole MIC at least 32 mg/L, amphotericin B at least 2 mg/L, and micafungin at least 4 mg/L. They are interim guides with uncertain outcome correlation, not universal susceptible breakpoints. The October 2026 CDC page notes an established CLSI C. auris-specific rezafungin breakpoint, in addition to the tentative thresholds for other agents. Ask the laboratory which method and interpretive standard it uses; do not transfer thresholds between drugs or methods. [46]
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Advanced clinical considerations Fellow teaching Species-specific susceptibility interpretation For C. glabrata, CLSI fluconazole results use susceptible-dose dependent or resistant categories rather than a standard susceptible category. A susceptible-dose dependent result requires an appropriate dose and exposure. Prior echinocandin treatment or persistent infection should prompt echinocandin testing and repeat evaluation for resistance. For C. parapsilosis, use species-specific interpretation: a naturally higher MIC does not by itself mean an echinocandin will fail. [1] Fellow teaching C. auris susceptibility thresholds CDC's tentative resistance thresholds include fluconazole MIC at least 32 mg/L, amphotericin B at least 2 mg/L, and micafungin at least 4 mg/L. They are interim guides with uncertain outcome correlation, not universal susceptible breakpoints. The October 2026 CDC page notes an established CLSI C. auris-specific rezafungin breakpoint, in addition to the tentative thresholds for other agents. Ask the laboratory which method and interpretive standard it uses; do not transfer thresholds between drugs or methods. [46] Fellow teaching Dematiaceous molds Melanized molds such as Alternaria, Curvularia, Exophiala, and Cladophialophora differ in susceptibility, syndrome, and optimal therapy. Itraconazole, voriconazole, and posaconazole have activity against many species, with species-specific variation. Isavuconazole has variable in vitro activity with less clinical evidence; fluconazole is unreliable. CNS disease requires attention to penetration, species identification, susceptibility results, and surgical source control. Isavuconazole susceptibility cannot be inferred from results for voriconazole or posaconazole. [43] [44] The VITAL cryptococcosis/endemic-fungus subset included only 38 patients across five genera and had no randomized comparator. Comparative efficacy for each organism remains uncertain. [42] Fellow teaching Echinocandin resistance FKS mutations can confer class resistance. Prior echinocandin exposure, persistent candidemia, and species identification affect the need for susceptibility testing. C. parapsilosis has higher baseline echinocandin MICs, but that alone does not establish treatment failure. Request susceptibility data and interpret the breakpoint for that species and drug. [1] Fellow teaching CSF and brain tissue concentrations Meningitis, an angioinvasive lesion, and an encapsulated abscess are different compartments. Isavuconazole tissue measurements from two patients showed substantially different concentrations in inflamed versus normal brain. Amphotericin B can be effective in CNS infection despite low CSF levels. A concentration in homogenized tissue does not establish free extracellular exposure or comparative clinical efficacy. [16] [1] Fellow teaching Parent-only and combined itraconazole targets The 2026 IDSA aspergillosis pharmacology appendix describes combined parent-plus-hydroxy targets, whereas current IDSA histoplasmosis guidance favors a parent component >1 mg/L and <3-4 mg/L, and states that a universal combined cutoff has not been established. It notes that combined levels >2 mg/L may provide similar responses to parent levels >1 mg/L. Mayo also provides distinct parent and combined interpretation. State the assay and treatment target explicitly. A combined result can meet its target while the parent level remains below a parent-only target. [3] [12] [13]

slides.title: Dematiaceous molds
paragraphs: The VITAL cryptococcosis/endemic-fungus subset included only 38 patients across five genera and had no randomized comparator. Comparative efficacy for each organism remains uncertain. [42]
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Advanced clinical considerations Fellow teaching Species-specific susceptibility interpretation For C. glabrata, CLSI fluconazole results use susceptible-dose dependent or resistant categories rather than a standard susceptible category. A susceptible-dose dependent result requires an appropriate dose and exposure. Prior echinocandin treatment or persistent infection should prompt echinocandin testing and repeat evaluation for resistance. For C. parapsilosis, use species-specific interpretation: a naturally higher MIC does not by itself mean an echinocandin will fail. [1] Fellow teaching C. auris susceptibility thresholds CDC's tentative resistance thresholds include fluconazole MIC at least 32 mg/L, amphotericin B at least 2 mg/L, and micafungin at least 4 mg/L. They are interim guides with uncertain outcome correlation, not universal susceptible breakpoints. The October 2026 CDC page notes an established CLSI C. auris-specific rezafungin breakpoint, in addition to the tentative thresholds for other agents. Ask the laboratory which method and interpretive standard it uses; do not transfer thresholds between drugs or methods. [46] Fellow teaching Dematiaceous molds Melanized molds such as Alternaria, Curvularia, Exophiala, and Cladophialophora differ in susceptibility, syndrome, and optimal therapy. Itraconazole, voriconazole, and posaconazole have activity against many species, with species-specific variation. Isavuconazole has variable in vitro activity with less clinical evidence; fluconazole is unreliable. CNS disease requires attention to penetration, species identification, susceptibility results, and surgical source control. Isavuconazole susceptibility cannot be inferred from results for voriconazole or posaconazole. [43] [44] The VITAL cryptococcosis/endemic-fungus subset included only 38 patients across five genera and had no randomized comparator. Comparative efficacy for each organism remains uncertain. [42] Fellow teaching Echinocandin resistance FKS mutations can confer class resistance. Prior echinocandin exposure, persistent candidemia, and species identification affect the need for susceptibility testing. C. parapsilosis has higher baseline echinocandin MICs, but that alone does not establish treatment failure. Request susceptibility data and interpret the breakpoint for that species and drug. [1] Fellow teaching CSF and brain tissue concentrations Meningitis, an angioinvasive lesion, and an encapsulated abscess are different compartments. Isavuconazole tissue measurements from two patients showed substantially different concentrations in inflamed versus normal brain. Amphotericin B can be effective in CNS infection despite low CSF levels. A concentration in homogenized tissue does not establish free extracellular exposure or comparative clinical efficacy. [16] [1] Fellow teaching Parent-only and combined itraconazole targets The 2026 IDSA aspergillosis pharmacology appendix describes combined parent-plus-hydroxy targets, whereas current IDSA histoplasmosis guidance favors a parent component >1 mg/L and <3-4 mg/L, and states that a universal combined cutoff has not been established. It notes that combined levels >2 mg/L may provide similar responses to parent levels >1 mg/L. Mayo also provides distinct parent and combined interpretation. State the assay and treatment target explicitly. A combined result can meet its target while the parent level remains below a parent-only target. [3] [12] [13]

slides.title: Echinocandin resistance
paragraphs: Fellow teaching
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Advanced clinical considerations Fellow teaching Species-specific susceptibility interpretation For C. glabrata, CLSI fluconazole results use susceptible-dose dependent or resistant categories rather than a standard susceptible category. A susceptible-dose dependent result requires an appropriate dose and exposure. Prior echinocandin treatment or persistent infection should prompt echinocandin testing and repeat evaluation for resistance. For C. parapsilosis, use species-specific interpretation: a naturally higher MIC does not by itself mean an echinocandin will fail. [1] Fellow teaching C. auris susceptibility thresholds CDC's tentative resistance thresholds include fluconazole MIC at least 32 mg/L, amphotericin B at least 2 mg/L, and micafungin at least 4 mg/L. They are interim guides with uncertain outcome correlation, not universal susceptible breakpoints. The October 2026 CDC page notes an established CLSI C. auris-specific rezafungin breakpoint, in addition to the tentative thresholds for other agents. Ask the laboratory which method and interpretive standard it uses; do not transfer thresholds between drugs or methods. [46] Fellow teaching Dematiaceous molds Melanized molds such as Alternaria, Curvularia, Exophiala, and Cladophialophora differ in susceptibility, syndrome, and optimal therapy. Itraconazole, voriconazole, and posaconazole have activity against many species, with species-specific variation. Isavuconazole has variable in vitro activity with less clinical evidence; fluconazole is unreliable. CNS disease requires attention to penetration, species identification, susceptibility results, and surgical source control. Isavuconazole susceptibility cannot be inferred from results for voriconazole or posaconazole. [43] [44] The VITAL cryptococcosis/endemic-fungus subset included only 38 patients across five genera and had no randomized comparator. Comparative efficacy for each organism remains uncertain. [42] Fellow teaching Echinocandin resistance FKS mutations can confer class resistance. Prior echinocandin exposure, persistent candidemia, and species identification affect the need for susceptibility testing. C. parapsilosis has higher baseline echinocandin MICs, but that alone does not establish treatment failure. Request susceptibility data and interpret the breakpoint for that species and drug. [1] Fellow teaching CSF and brain tissue concentrations Meningitis, an angioinvasive lesion, and an encapsulated abscess are different compartments. Isavuconazole tissue measurements from two patients showed substantially different concentrations in inflamed versus normal brain. Amphotericin B can be effective in CNS infection despite low CSF levels. A concentration in homogenized tissue does not establish free extracellular exposure or comparative clinical efficacy. [16] [1] Fellow teaching Parent-only and combined itraconazole targets The 2026 IDSA aspergillosis pharmacology appendix describes combined parent-plus-hydroxy targets, whereas current IDSA histoplasmosis guidance favors a parent component >1 mg/L and <3-4 mg/L, and states that a universal combined cutoff has not been established. It notes that combined levels >2 mg/L may provide similar responses to parent levels >1 mg/L. Mayo also provides distinct parent and combined interpretation. State the assay and treatment target explicitly. A combined result can meet its target while the parent level remains below a parent-only target. [3] [12] [13]

slides.title: Parent-only and combined itraconazole targets
paragraphs: The 2026 IDSA aspergillosis pharmacology appendix describes combined parent-plus-hydroxy targets, whereas current IDSA histoplasmosis guidance favors a parent component >1 mg/L and <3-4 mg/L, and states that a universal combined cutoff has not been established. It notes that combined levels >2 mg/L may provide similar responses to parent levels >1 mg/L. Mayo also provides distinct parent and combined interpretation. State the assay and treatment target explicitly. A combined result can meet its target while the parent level remains below a parent-only target. [3] [12] [13]
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Advanced clinical considerations Fellow teaching Species-specific susceptibility interpretation For C. glabrata, CLSI fluconazole results use susceptible-dose dependent or resistant categories rather than a standard susceptible category. A susceptible-dose dependent result requires an appropriate dose and exposure. Prior echinocandin treatment or persistent infection should prompt echinocandin testing and repeat evaluation for resistance. For C. parapsilosis, use species-specific interpretation: a naturally higher MIC does not by itself mean an echinocandin will fail. [1] Fellow teaching C. auris susceptibility thresholds CDC's tentative resistance thresholds include fluconazole MIC at least 32 mg/L, amphotericin B at least 2 mg/L, and micafungin at least 4 mg/L. They are interim guides with uncertain outcome correlation, not universal susceptible breakpoints. The October 2026 CDC page notes an established CLSI C. auris-specific rezafungin breakpoint, in addition to the tentative thresholds for other agents. Ask the laboratory which method and interpretive standard it uses; do not transfer thresholds between drugs or methods. [46] Fellow teaching Dematiaceous molds Melanized molds such as Alternaria, Curvularia, Exophiala, and Cladophialophora differ in susceptibility, syndrome, and optimal therapy. Itraconazole, voriconazole, and posaconazole have activity against many species, with species-specific variation. Isavuconazole has variable in vitro activity with less clinical evidence; fluconazole is unreliable. CNS disease requires attention to penetration, species identification, susceptibility results, and surgical source control. Isavuconazole susceptibility cannot be inferred from results for voriconazole or posaconazole. [43] [44] The VITAL cryptococcosis/endemic-fungus subset included only 38 patients across five genera and had no randomized comparator. Comparative efficacy for each organism remains uncertain. [42] Fellow teaching Echinocandin resistance FKS mutations can confer class resistance. Prior echinocandin exposure, persistent candidemia, and species identification affect the need for susceptibility testing. C. parapsilosis has higher baseline echinocandin MICs, but that alone does not establish treatment failure. Request susceptibility data and interpret the breakpoint for that species and drug. [1] Fellow teaching CSF and brain tissue concentrations Meningitis, an angioinvasive lesion, and an encapsulated abscess are different compartments. Isavuconazole tissue measurements from two patients showed substantially different concentrations in inflamed versus normal brain. Amphotericin B can be effective in CNS infection despite low CSF levels. A concentration in homogenized tissue does not establish free extracellular exposure or comparative clinical efficacy. [16] [1] Fellow teaching Parent-only and combined itraconazole targets The 2026 IDSA aspergillosis pharmacology appendix describes combined parent-plus-hydroxy targets, whereas current IDSA histoplasmosis guidance favors a parent component >1 mg/L and <3-4 mg/L, and states that a universal combined cutoff has not been established. It notes that combined levels >2 mg/L may provide similar responses to parent levels >1 mg/L. Mayo also provides distinct parent and combined interpretation. State the assay and treatment target explicitly. A combined result can meet its target while the parent level remains below a parent-only target. [3] [12] [13]

slides.title: Voriconazole versus itraconazole in histoplasmosis
paragraphs: A single-center retrospective cohort compared 175 itraconazole-treated patients with 19 voriconazole-treated patients. Voriconazole was associated with higher mortality during the first 42 days after treatment initiation (adjusted hazard ratio 4.30; 95% CI 1.3-13.9). The small voriconazole group, nonrandomized treatment assignment, and potential residual confounding limit causal inference. These findings support itraconazole preference and argue against treating voriconazole as an interchangeable alternative. [56]
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Key studies Voriconazole versus itraconazole in histoplasmosis A single-center retrospective cohort compared 175 itraconazole-treated patients with 19 voriconazole-treated patients. Voriconazole was associated with higher mortality during the first 42 days after treatment initiation (adjusted hazard ratio 4.30; 95% CI 1.3-13.9). The small voriconazole group, nonrandomized treatment assignment, and potential residual confounding limit causal inference. These findings support itraconazole preference and argue against treating voriconazole as an interchangeable alternative. [56] Isavuconazole versus voriconazole: SECURE Day-42 mortality was 19% with isavuconazole versus 20% with voriconazole, meeting noninferiority. Drug-related adverse events were less frequent with isavuconazole. The trial did not establish superiority or equivalence for every rare mold or CNS infection. [20] Posaconazole for primary invasive aspergillosis treatment The 2021 randomized trial met noninferiority versus voriconazole for primary invasive aspergillosis treatment. Day-42 mortality was 15% versus 21% in the intention-to-treat population. The confidence interval for the treatment difference crossed zero, so mortality superiority was not established. The regimen used modern IV/tablet formulations, not conventional suspension. [21] Voriconazole TDM trials A 110-patient single-center randomized study supported voriconazole TDM, with less discontinuation from toxicity and better treatment response. A later multicenter cluster randomized crossover study did not show improved treatment outcomes with TDM-guided dosing. PK variability and exposure-related toxicity support monitoring, although a consistent survival benefit has not been shown. [22] [23]

slides.title: Posaconazole for primary invasive aspergillosis treatment
paragraphs: The 2021 randomized trial met noninferiority versus voriconazole for primary invasive aspergillosis treatment. Day-42 mortality was 15% versus 21% in the intention-to-treat population. The confidence interval for the treatment difference crossed zero, so mortality superiority was not established. The regimen used modern IV/tablet formulations, not conventional suspension. [21]
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Key studies Voriconazole versus itraconazole in histoplasmosis A single-center retrospective cohort compared 175 itraconazole-treated patients with 19 voriconazole-treated patients. Voriconazole was associated with higher mortality during the first 42 days after treatment initiation (adjusted hazard ratio 4.30; 95% CI 1.3-13.9). The small voriconazole group, nonrandomized treatment assignment, and potential residual confounding limit causal inference. These findings support itraconazole preference and argue against treating voriconazole as an interchangeable alternative. [56] Isavuconazole versus voriconazole: SECURE Day-42 mortality was 19% with isavuconazole versus 20% with voriconazole, meeting noninferiority. Drug-related adverse events were less frequent with isavuconazole. The trial did not establish superiority or equivalence for every rare mold or CNS infection. [20] Posaconazole for primary invasive aspergillosis treatment The 2021 randomized trial met noninferiority versus voriconazole for primary invasive aspergillosis treatment. Day-42 mortality was 15% versus 21% in the intention-to-treat population. The confidence interval for the treatment difference crossed zero, so mortality superiority was not established. The regimen used modern IV/tablet formulations, not conventional suspension. [21] Voriconazole TDM trials A 110-patient single-center randomized study supported voriconazole TDM, with less discontinuation from toxicity and better treatment response. A later multicenter cluster randomized crossover study did not show improved treatment outcomes with TDM-guided dosing. PK variability and exposure-related toxicity support monitoring, although a consistent survival benefit has not been shown. [22] [23]
